title: Production, immediate sales, returns and schedules

processes.title: Make-to-Order
processes.memory_hook: The sales order creates its own supply segment.

sap_scope_items.label: Make-to-Order Production – Finished Goods Sales and Final Assembly

processes.business_intent: Manufacture or procure supply specifically for an individual sales-order requirement rather than serving demand from generic stock.

control_plane.why: creates individual sales-order demand and valuation behavior
defines how stock and production costs are valued
changes how supply is created and scheduled

data_hinges.changes: planning segment, account assignment and special stock

impact_summary: Customer demand propagates into production/procurement and creates stock that normally cannot satisfy other sales orders.
constraints: Order-specific stock is intentionally not interchangeable.
Costing and valuation design differs by MTO variant.
Advanced planning variants have additional prerequisites.
lead_questions: Where is the customer-specific boundary: planning, stock, costing, or all three?
What happens if the customer changes quantity after supply exists?
Can leftover stock be reused and under what governance?

processes.title: Cash Sales
processes.memory_hook: Order, hand over, and take payment almost at once.
processes.business_intent: Handle immediate sale and pickup/payment where the delivery is created immediately and receivables are not managed like a standard credit sale.

control_plane.why: triggers immediate delivery and cash-oriented billing behavior
depends on whether goods are already handed over or picked from warehouse
billing requires consistency between order and goods issue quantity

data_hinges.changes: whether the cash sale can be billed

impact_summary: Collapses time between order and delivery and changes the receivables model; it is not simply a standard order with faster warehouse processing.
constraints: Exceptions often need manual intervention because the business promise is immediate.
lead_questions: Do we really need cash-sales semantics or only fast delivery?
What happens when stock is short after payment?
Where is the payment confirmation represented?

processes.title: Rush Order
processes.business_intent: Create a sales order that automatically creates an immediate delivery while keeping normal delivery-related billing later.

control_plane.why: decides what can actually be delivered now
keeps invoicing after execution rather than at order entry

data_hinges.changes: what goes into the immediate delivery
when the later invoice becomes due

impact_summary: Accelerates logistics without adopting cash-sales accounting.
constraints: Unconfirmed quantity can fall into backorder processing.
Same-day business expectation magnifies master-data and ATP errors.
lead_questions: Why rush instead of standard SFS with priority?
Which block is allowed in a process marketed as immediate?

processes.title: Customer Returns
processes.memory_hook: The outbound flow runs backward, but disposition decides what happens next.
processes.business_intent: Bring goods back from the customer, inspect or classify them, choose a logistical follow-up, and compensate the customer by credit or replacement.

control_plane.why: selects lean versus more comprehensive returns processing
links reason, quantity and commercial history
decides stock, scrap, supplier return, repair or replacement

impact_summary: Inventory, quality, accounting and customer-service decisions converge; the credit memo is only one possible end state.
constraints: Direct customer-to-supplier returns and complex inspection flows need the appropriate variant.
Reference and approval rules can restrict what users may return or refund.
lead_questions: What is the disposition decision, not just the return reason?
Can returned stock re-enter available inventory?
Where do repeated return patterns become a master-data or quality problem?

processes.title: Sales Scheduling Agreements
processes.memory_hook: We receive a rolling delivery signal instead of creating a separate customer order for every call-off.
processes.business_intent: We use a sales scheduling agreement when the customer repeatedly sends concrete delivery requirements over time and we need delivery schedules, schedule lines, cumulative quantities, and optional forecast/JIT/planning layers.

control_plane.why: we define the long-term sales document and the supported logistics behavior
we separate forecast, JIT and planning signals according to the planning horizon
we keep the concrete quantities and dates that drive delivery execution
we reconcile what the customer requested, what we received as a release and what we already delivered
we can receive delivery schedules from the buyer and update the corresponding sales scheduling agreement

data_hinges.changes: what we make due for delivery and when
the planning horizon and operational precision of the demand signal
how we reconcile repeated releases over a long-running agreement
how we identify and execute the customer's recurring demand

impact_summary: We replace repeated discrete order entry with an evolving delivery signal. The operational quantities and dates live in the scheduling agreement schedule lines, so the normal flow does not need a separate release-order sales order.
We treat cumulative-quantity reconciliation and integration quality as part of the core process because a wrong signal can create false demand or false completion.
constraints: We distinguish sales scheduling agreements from purchase scheduling agreements; they represent opposite sides of the customer-supplier relationship.
We govern forecast, JIT and planning horizons explicitly.
We treat cumulative-quantity mismatches as operational defects because they can create false demand or false completion.
When we integrate external buyer schedules, we design message identity, duplicate handling, recovery and reconciliation together.
For very long-running agreements, we watch document-flow volume because years of follow-on documents can affect performance.
lead_questions: Do we need separate call-off orders, or does the customer already send a rolling delivery schedule?
Which schedule do we treat as operationally binding: forecast, JIT or planning?
How do we reconcile cumulative quantities between customer and supplier?
How does a schedule line become delivery due?
What do we do when forecast and JIT signals conflict?
How do we recover when an external delivery schedule is missing, duplicated or inconsistent?
